extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, journal editors, and the interested public (health policy/community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and arguments about whether and how clinical researchers should make raw clinical/trial data publicly available, especially as a condition of journal publication. Covers editorial policy proposals, practical examples, privacy concerns, and cultural motivations for withholding data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public data sharing as condition of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The world's leading medical journals have a proposal that researchers would have to publicly share their clinical data to get their studies published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an editorial policy change that could transform medical science by making data sharing a requirement for publication; the proposal is framed as something journals can adopt to increase openness and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show your work / let other people see the raw data
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the basic principles is 'show your work. Let other people see it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a basic scientific norm — other fields routinely allow others to inspect primary data (analogy to astronomers and telescopes) — and medicine should do the same to permit independent inspection and use of original data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide underlying data to enable reproduction and building on results
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers need to share the underlying data — the basic facts — in order for others to build on that work, replicate analyses, or challenge conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without access to raw data, others are 'walled off' and cannot verify, extend, or overturn findings. Data sharing is necessary for the cumulative progress of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not withhold data to preserve future publication opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Withholding data is often motivated by the desire to continue publishing from the same data set; investigators may be reluctant to allow others to 'peer into the insides' to protect future publishing opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames this motive as understandable but ultimately not a good reason to hoard data; encouraging norms/policies should prevent researchers from blocking access simply to retain future publishing advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and protect patient privacy when sharing clinical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient privacy concerns must be respected when clinical data are shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data-sharing policies should include safeguards to protect privacy (de-identification, governance), balancing openness with confidentiality; privacy concerns are acknowledged as a primary caveat to broad data release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established repositories for trial data (e.g., NIH repository)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit trial data in recognized repositories — for example, the NIH has a repository of trials and the author returned data to NIH for sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical mechanism: trusted repositories can host and manage access to shared clinical trial data; journals or funders can require deposit into such repositories as part of publication or funding terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make data available in a timely manner after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'Within a year of publishing that study, we made that data available.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents timely release (the author's own trial data was shared within a year) as a model; policies should encourage prompt sharing rather than long delays that impede verification and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow independent reanalysis and accept that others may reach different conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should not be afraid that others will draw conclusions they disagree with — independent analysis is precisely the point of sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open data enables others to demonstrate if conclusions are unsupported; the possibility of disagreement is framed as healthy and necessary for scientific self-correction rather than a reason to restrict access.
